To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
fine motor skills at Age 3 predicted expressive language development through Age 19, in two independent cohorts of preschoolers with ASD who were language delayed.

fine motor skills at age three are a predictor of expressive language development at age 19 in preschoolers with ASD who use less than single words at age three, but this is not the case for preschoolers who use single words at age 3.
Marked fine motor delays at age 3 years are a strong predictor of later expressive language development in preschoolers with autism spectrum disorder.

the early identification of children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).
identifying the early predictors of later language outcomes in children with ASD.
understanding the development of language skills in children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) from preschool through school age and early adulthood.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the study of predictors of longer term expressive language development in two independent longitudinal cohort of language delayed preschooler with Autism Spectrum Disorder is a critical step in identifying those children who are at risk of persistent language impairment.
fine motor skills at age 3 is the best predictor of longer term development.

the findings of this paper are important for understanding the predictors of longer term development in language impaired children with autism, and that the results of the study are important for informing the identification and treatment of children at risk of persistent language impairments.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
early fine motor delays in ASD may be a marker of risk for persistent language impairment.
early motor and joint attention skills may provide important cues for longer term expressive language outcomes.
early motor and social skills are important to monitor and target in intervention for children with language delays.
The main takeaway from our work is that
children with autism who are not using single words or more by age 3 are at risk for not developing expressive language by age 19.
fine motor skills may serve as a proxy for identifying language delayed preschoolers at risk for persistent impairments.
children with ASD who have language delays and poor fine motor skills are at risk of persistent language delays, even if other aspects of development are not severely impaired.
